Making the Bond: Lugs, Connectors, Routing, Labels, Checks

Unit 3: Pathways and Spaces. Lesson 14 of 52 in INST1 Academy.

The electrician hands you a spool of green 6 AWG and says the busbar is yours. A bond is only as good as its worst joint, and a joint made on painted metal is not a bond at all.

The connection

Step                What to do
Lug                 two-hole compression lug on every busbar and rack connection
Surface             scrape paint to bare metal
Compound            apply antioxidant, then bolt the connection
Hardware            star washers and the right screws for the equipment threads

Do not use a lug made for a different wire size. A compression lug is crimped with the right die, not squeezed with pliers.

Routing

  • Take the shortest path, with no sharp bends. The minimum bend radius is 203 mm (8 in), and never bend a conductor to less than 90 degrees.
  • Mount the busbar on insulated standoffs with at least 51 mm (2 in) of clearance behind it.
  • Never daisy-chain rack to rack. Each rack gets its own conductor back to the busbar.
  • Metal conduit and tray are bonded; a grounding bushing carries a 6 AWG copper wire to the busbar.

Labels

Label both ends of every bonding conductor, in the same scheme as the rest of the job, so that the next tech can follow each conductor without opening the room.

Checks

Make a visual check: tight, clean, correct lug, correct color, no sharp bends. Then a continuity check. Two-point bonding resistance is recommended at 0.1 ohm (100 milliohms) at most. The electrician or the testing technician verifies resistance; you do not guess it.

Who owns the final tie

Only a qualified electrician connects to the ac panel ground or the service ground. Your job ends at the telecom busbar.

Tip: keep a small bottle of antioxidant compound in the bag. A dry joint fails a test on day one.
Exam tip: bare metal, antioxidant, compression lug, shortest path, no daisy chain, and both ends labeled.
Remember
Scrape to bare metal, antioxidant, two-hole compression lugs, shortest route, no daisy chains, label both ends, and let the right person verify resistance.
Deeper explanation

Making the Bond: Lugs, Connectors, Routing, Labels, Checks, explained slowly

A bond that passes the first time

A good bond is a short list of steps done in the same order every time. The mistakes are almost always shortcuts: paint left on, a lug squeezed with pliers, or a conductor bent around a corner.

Step   Action                                       Why
1      Cut the conductor to the shortest route      less resistance and less to go wrong
2      Strip and install a compression lug          a crimp the right die closes
3      Scrape the metal to bare metal               paint insulates
4      Apply antioxidant compound                   keeps oxide off the joint
5      Bolt with a two-hole lug, star washers       two holes resist twisting
6      Label both ends                              the next tech can follow it
7      Check visually and for continuity            proves the joint

Routing rules

  • Minimum bend radius 203 mm (8 in). Never bend a conductor to less than 90 degrees.
  • Mount the busbar on insulated standoffs with at least 51 mm (2 in) of clearance behind it.
  • Keep conductors away from sharp edges.
  • No daisy-chaining. Each rack goes back to the busbar on its own conductor.

Worked example: reading a resistance check

After the bonding is complete, the testing technician or the electrician measures the two-point bonding resistance between the busbar and the rack. The recommended maximum is 0.1 ohm (100 milliohms).

Rack   Reading       Result    Likely cause if it fails
1      0.04 ohm      pass
2      0.06 ohm      pass
3      0.35 ohm      fail      paint under the lug, or no antioxidant
4      open circuit  fail      conductor not connected

Rack 3 fails. The visual check finds a lug on painted metal. You loosen it, scrape the paint to bare metal, apply antioxidant, and tighten. The tech measures again and records 0.05 ohm.

Who owns what

You make and label the telecom bond. The electrician makes any connection to an ac panel or service ground, because only qualified electricians connect there. The electrician or the testing technician verifies resistance and records it.

Remember: bare metal, antioxidant, compression lug, shortest route, labels at both ends.
